chapter_text:
CHAPTER 12 - CONCURRENT LINES

Introduction

In earlier chapters you studied straight lines, triangles and their many properties. Two distinct straight lines in a plane either meet at exactly one point (they are intersecting) or never meet (they are parallel). But an interesting situation arises when we look at THREE or more lines together. Sometimes three lines are so specially placed that they all pass through one and the same point. Such lines are called CONCURRENT LINES, and the common point through which they all pass is called the POINT OF CONCURRENCY.

This chapter studies concurrency in the setting where it matters most in school geometry: the triangle. A triangle has four famous sets of three special lines (or line segments), and in every one of these four sets the three lines are concurrent. These four points of concurrency are the CENTROID, the ORTHOCENTRE, the CIRCUMCENTRE and the INCENTRE - together often called the 'four classic centres' of a triangle. We shall meet each of them, learn how it is constructed, state its main properties, and see where it lies for acute, right and obtuse triangles.

12.1 CONCURRENT LINES AND THE POINT OF CONCURRENCY

Three or more lines in a plane are said to be CONCURRENT if they all pass through one common point. That common point is the POINT OF CONCURRENCY (also called the point of concurrence).

Compare the following:
 - Two lines that cross meet at a single point - but two lines are never called 'concurrent'; concurrency needs at least three lines.
 - Three lines drawn at random will usually form a triangle - each pair meets at a different point, giving three separate intersection points. These lines are NOT concurrent.
 - If, however, the three lines have been chosen so that all three intersection points coincide into ONE point, the lines are concurrent.

So concurrency is a special, non-accidental property. For example, the three lines x = 0 (the y-axis), y = 0 (the x-axis) and y = x are NOT concurrent as a set of three general lines - but the x-axis, the y-axis and the line y = x all pass through the origin (0, 0), so in fact they ARE concurrent, meeting at the origin.

To TEST three lines for concurrency, a common method is:
 (1) Find the point of intersection of any two of the lines.
 (2) Check whether that point lies on the third line.
If it does, the three lines are concurrent; the intersection point is the point of concurrency. If it does not, they are not concurrent.

The remarkable fact of triangle geometry is that four particular triples of lines are ALWAYS concurrent, no matter what triangle you start with. We take them one at a time.

12.2 MEDIANS AND THE CENTROID

A MEDIAN of a triangle is a line segment joining a VERTEX to the MID-POINT of the OPPOSITE SIDE. Every triangle has exactly three medians, one from each vertex.

Consider triangle ABC. Let D be the mid-point of BC, E the mid-point of CA, and F the mid-point of AB. Then AD, BE and CF are the three medians. These three medians are concurrent; their common point is called the CENTROID, usually denoted by G.

The centroid has a beautiful and important property - the 2 : 1 RATIO PROPERTY:

  The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, measured from the vertex.

That is, on median AD we have AG : GD = 2 : 1; on median BE we have BG : GE = 2 : 1; and on median CF we have CG : GF = 2 : 1. In each case the longer part (2 parts) is next to the vertex and the shorter part (1 part) is next to the mid-point of the side. So the distance from a vertex to the centroid is twice the distance from the centroid to the mid-point of the opposite side; equivalently the centroid is two-thirds of the way along each median from the vertex.

Positions and further facts about the centroid:
 - The centroid ALWAYS lies INSIDE the triangle - for every triangle, acute, right or obtuse.
 - The centroid is the 'centre of gravity' (centre of mass) of a uniform triangular lamina; a triangle balances on a pin placed at G.
 - In coordinate geometry, if the vertices are A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3), then the centroid is
       G = ( (x1 + x2 + x3)/3 , (y1 + y2 + y3)/3 ).
 - Each median divides the triangle into two smaller triangles of EQUAL AREA, and the three medians together divide the triangle into six smaller triangles of equal area.

12.3 ALTITUDES AND THE ORTHOCENTRE

An ALTITUDE of a triangle is the PERPENDICULAR segment drawn from a VERTEX to the LINE containing the OPPOSITE SIDE. It measures the 'height' of the triangle from that vertex. Every triangle has three altitudes, one from each vertex.

In triangle ABC, drop a perpendicular from A to BC, from B to CA, and from C to AB. These three altitudes are concurrent; their common point is the ORTHOCENTRE, usually denoted by H.

Positions of the orthocentre depend on the type of triangle:
 - In an ACUTE triangle (all angles less than 90 degrees), the orthocentre lies INSIDE the triangle.
 - In a RIGHT triangle, the orthocentre lies exactly AT the vertex of the RIGHT ANGLE. (This is because the two legs of a right triangle are themselves altitudes, and they meet at the right-angle vertex.)
 - In an OBTUSE triangle (one angle greater than 90 degrees), the orthocentre lies OUTSIDE the triangle. To find it, the sides must be extended so that the perpendiculars from the vertices can meet outside.

Note that an altitude is different from a median: an altitude is drawn perpendicular to the opposite side (and need not reach its mid-point), whereas a median reaches the mid-point of the opposite side (and need not be perpendicular). Only in special triangles (for example an equilateral triangle, or the altitude/median from the apex of an isosceles triangle) do they coincide.

12.4 PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS AND THE CIRCUMCENTRE

The PERPENDICULAR BISECTOR of a side of a triangle is the line that passes through the MID-POINT of that side and is PERPENDICULAR to it. Every triangle has three such perpendicular bisectors, one for each side.

The key idea behind this centre is a property of the perpendicular bisector of a segment: EVERY point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is EQUIDISTANT from the two end-points of the segment (and, conversely, every point equidistant from the two ends lies on the perpendicular bisector).

In triangle ABC, the three perpendicular bisectors of the sides are concurrent; their common point is the CIRCUMCENTRE, usually denoted by O (or S). Because O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC it is equidistant from B and C; because it lies on the perpendicular bisector of CA it is equidistant from C and A. Hence O is equidistant from ALL THREE vertices:
       OA = OB = OC = R.
This common distance R is the CIRCUMRADIUS. A circle drawn with centre O and radius R passes through all three vertices A, B and C. This circle is the CIRCUMCIRCLE (or circumscribed circle) of the triangle - the unique circle passing through the three vertices.

Positions of the circumcentre:
 - In an ACUTE triangle, the circumcentre lies INSIDE the triangle.
 - In a RIGHT triangle, the circumcentre lies exactly AT the MID-POINT of the HYPOTENUSE. (Consequently, in a right triangle the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle, and the circumradius equals half the hypotenuse.)
 - In an OBTUSE triangle, the circumcentre lies OUTSIDE the triangle.

12.5 ANGLE BISECTORS AND THE INCENTRE

The (internal) ANGLE BISECTOR of an angle of a triangle is the line segment (or ray) that divides the angle into two equal halves, drawn from the vertex into the interior of the triangle. Every triangle has three internal angle bisectors, one at each vertex.

The key idea behind this centre is a property of an angle bisector: EVERY point on the bisector of an angle is EQUIDISTANT from the two ARMS (sides) of the angle, the distance being measured along the perpendicular to each arm.

In triangle ABC, the three internal angle bisectors are concurrent; their common point is the INCENTRE, usually denoted by I. Because I lies on the bisector of angle B it is equidistant from sides BA and BC; because it lies on the bisector of angle C it is equidistant from sides CB and CA. Hence I is equidistant from ALL THREE sides of the triangle. That common perpendicular distance is the INRADIUS, denoted r. A circle drawn with centre I and radius r touches (is tangent to) all three sides from inside; this circle is the INCIRCLE (or inscribed circle) of the triangle.

Position of the incentre:
 - The incentre ALWAYS lies INSIDE the triangle - for every triangle, whatever its type. This is natural, because the internal bisectors all head into the interior, and a circle that touches all three sides from within must have its centre inside.

12.6 PROPERTIES AND PROBLEMS ON TRIANGLE CENTRES

Let us gather the four centres and their essentials in one place:

  Centre        Lines that meet             Symbol   Key property                    Always inside?
  Centroid      3 medians                   G        divides each median 2:1         Yes
  Orthocentre   3 altitudes                 H        foot of the heights             No (acute:in, right:at right angle, obtuse:out)
  Circumcentre  3 perpendicular bisectors   O        OA=OB=OC=R; centre of circumcircle   No (acute:in, right:mid-hypotenuse, obtuse:out)
  Incentre      3 angle bisectors           I        equidistant from the 3 sides; centre of incircle   Yes

Two special results worth remembering:
 - EQUILATERAL TRIANGLE: all four centres COINCIDE at a single point. The medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors are the very same three lines, so G, H, O and I are one and the same point.
 - EULER LINE (for reference): in any triangle the centroid G, orthocentre H and circumcentre O are collinear (they lie on one straight line, the Euler line), and G divides the segment OH in the ratio OG : GH = 1 : 2. The incentre generally does NOT lie on the Euler line (except in the equilateral case).

Worked reasoning examples:
 (a) If AG = 8 cm where G is the centroid on median AD, find GD and AD. Since AG : GD = 2 : 1, GD = half of AG = 4 cm, and AD = AG + GD = 12 cm.
 (b) In a right triangle with the right angle at C, the orthocentre is at C itself, and the circumcentre is the mid-point of the hypotenuse AB; if AB = 10 cm then the circumradius R = 5 cm.
 (c) To find the circumcentre by construction, draw the perpendicular bisectors of any two sides; their intersection is O. To find the incentre, draw the bisectors of any two angles; their intersection is I.

SUMMARY

- Three or more lines are CONCURRENT if they all pass through one common point, the POINT OF CONCURRENCY. Test: find where two of the lines meet and check whether that point lies on the third.
- The three MEDIANS of a triangle meet at the CENTROID G, which divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex. G is always inside the triangle and is its centre of gravity.
- The three ALTITUDES meet at the ORTHOCENTRE H. It lies inside an acute triangle, at the right-angle vertex of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
- The three PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS of the sides meet at the CIRCUMCENTRE O, which is equidistant from the three vertices (OA = OB = OC = R) and is the centre of the circumcircle. It lies inside an acute triangle, at the mid-point of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
- The three ANGLE BISECTORS meet at the INCENTRE I, which is equidistant from the three sides (inradius r) and is the centre of the incircle. The incentre is always inside the triangle.
- In an EQUILATERAL triangle all four centres coincide. In general the centroid, orthocentre and circumcentre are collinear on the Euler line, with OG : GH = 1 : 2.

topics.name: Concurrent Lines and Point of Concurrency
topics.description: Meaning of concurrent lines (three or more lines through one common point); the point of concurrency; the method of testing three lines for concurrency by finding the intersection of two and checking the third.

topics.name: Medians and the Centroid
topics.description: A median joins a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side; the three medians are concurrent at the centroid G, which divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex and is the centre of gravity.

topics.name: Altitudes and the Orthocentre
topics.description: An altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side; the three altitudes are concurrent at the orthocentre H, whose position varies for acute, right and obtuse triangles.

topics.name: Perpendicular Bisectors and the Circumcentre
topics.description: The perpendicular bisector of a side passes through its mid-point perpendicularly; the three are concurrent at the circumcentre O, equidistant from all vertices and the centre of the circumcircle.

topics.name: Angle Bisectors and the Incentre
topics.description: An internal angle bisector divides an angle in half; the three are concurrent at the incentre I, equidistant from all three sides and the centre of the incircle, always inside the triangle.

topics.name: Properties and Problems on Triangle Centres
topics.description: Comparing the four centres, their positions for different triangle types, coincidence in the equilateral triangle, the Euler line, and solving simple numerical and reasoning problems on triangle centres.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Concurrent Lines and Point of Concurrency
learning_outcomes.description: Define concurrent lines and the point of concurrency, and test whether three given lines are concurrent by finding the intersection of two and checking the third.
Define a median and state that the three medians of a triangle are concurrent at the centroid, describing the centroid's position and role as centre of gravity.
Apply the 2:1 ratio property of the centroid to compute segment lengths along a median and locate the centroid in coordinate geometry.
Define an altitude, state that the three altitudes are concurrent at the orthocentre, and identify the orthocentre's position for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
Define the perpendicular bisector of a side, state that the three meet at the circumcentre, and use the equidistant-from-vertices property and the circumcircle.
Define an internal angle bisector, state that the three meet at the incentre, and use the equidistant-from-sides property and the incircle.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Properties and Problems on Triangle Centres
learning_outcomes.description: Compare the four triangle centres and their positions for different triangle types, including their coincidence in an equilateral triangle and collinearity on the Euler line.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Properties and Problems on Triangle Centres
learning_outcomes.description: Solve numerical and reasoning problems involving triangle centres, such as circumradius of a right triangle and constructions to locate the centres.

chapter_summary.title: Concurrent Lines - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter introduces concurrent lines - three or more lines that pass through a single common point called the point of concurrency. It then studies the four classic centres of a triangle formed by concurrent medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors, with their properties and positions.

sections.heading: Concurrent lines and point of concurrency
bullets: Three or more lines are concurrent when they all pass through one common point, called the point of concurrency.
Two lines are never called concurrent - concurrency requires at least three lines.
To test concurrency: find where two of the lines intersect, then check whether that point lies on the third line.
In a triangle, four special triples of lines are always concurrent - the medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors.

sections.heading: Medians and the centroid
bullets: A median joins a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side; every triangle has three medians.
The three medians are concurrent at the centroid G, which always lies inside the triangle.
The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1, measured from the vertex (the longer 2-part is next to the vertex).
In coordinates, G = ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3); G is the triangle's centre of gravity.

sections.heading: Altitudes and the orthocentre
bullets: An altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the line of the opposite side; every triangle has three altitudes.
The three altitudes are concurrent at the orthocentre H.
H lies inside an acute triangle, at the right-angle vertex of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
An altitude need not pass through the mid-point of the opposite side, so it generally differs from the median.

sections.heading: Perpendicular bisectors and the circumcentre
bullets: The perpendicular bisector of a side passes through its mid-point and is perpendicular to it.
The three perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre O, which is equidistant from the three vertices (OA = OB = OC = R).
O is the centre of the circumcircle, the circle through all three vertices; R is the circumradius.
O lies inside an acute triangle, at the mid-point of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.

sections.heading: Angle bisectors, the incentre and special results
bullets: An internal angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts; every point on it is equidistant from the two arms.
The three angle bisectors meet at the incentre I, which is equidistant from all three sides (inradius r) and always lies inside the triangle.
I is the centre of the incircle, the circle that touches all three sides from inside.
In an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide; in general G, H and O are collinear on the Euler line with OG:GH = 1:2.

key_takeaways: Concurrent lines pass through one common point, the point of concurrency; test by intersecting two lines and checking the third.
The three medians meet at the centroid G, which divides each median 2:1 from the vertex and is always inside the triangle.
The three altitudes meet at the orthocentre H - inside for acute, at the right-angle vertex for right, outside for obtuse triangles.
The three perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre O, equidistant from all vertices and the centre of the circumcircle.
The three angle bisectors meet at the incentre I, equidistant from all sides, the centre of the incircle, always inside the triangle.
In an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide; in general G, H and O are collinear on the Euler line (OG:GH = 1:2).

glossary.definition: Three or more lines in a plane that all pass through one common point.
The single common point through which a set of concurrent lines all pass.
A line segment joining a vertex of a triangle to the mid-point of the opposite side.
The point of concurrency of the three medians of a triangle; divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex. Denoted G.
The perpendicular segment from a vertex of a triangle to the line containing the opposite side.
The point of concurrency of the three altitudes of a triangle. Denoted H.
The line through the mid-point of a segment that is perpendicular to it; its points are equidistant from the segment's ends.
The point of concurrency of the three perpendicular bisectors of the sides; equidistant from the three vertices. Denoted O.
The circle passing through all three vertices of a triangle; its centre is the circumcentre and radius is the circumradius R.
A line or ray that divides an angle into two equal parts; its points are equidistant from the two arms of the angle.
The point of concurrency of the three internal angle bisectors; equidistant from the three sides. Always inside the triangle. Denoted I.
The circle that touches all three sides of a triangle from inside; its centre is the incentre and radius is the inradius r.
The radius R of the circumcircle; the common distance from the circumcentre to each vertex (OA = OB = OC = R).
The radius r of the incircle; the common perpendicular distance from the incentre to each of the three sides.
The straight line on which the centroid, orthocentre and circumcentre of a triangle lie, with OG:GH = 1:2.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Concurrent Lines (NIOS Mathematics Class 10)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw rough figures where helpful and show the reasoning steps. Marks are indicated against each question.

questions.question: Define concurrent lines and the point of concurrency. Give one example of three concurrent lines.
questions.answer: Three or more lines in a plane are said to be CONCURRENT if they all pass through one common point. That common point is called the POINT OF CONCURRENCY. Example: the x-axis, the y-axis and the line y = x all pass through the origin (0, 0), so they are concurrent, with the origin as the point of concurrency.
questions.explanation: Definition plus a valid example of three lines through one point.

questions.question: What is a median of a triangle? Name the point where the three medians meet and state its position relative to the triangle.
questions.answer: A MEDIAN is a line segment joining a VERTEX of a triangle to the MID-POINT of the OPPOSITE SIDE. Every triangle has three medians. The three medians are concurrent; their common point is the CENTROID (denoted G). The centroid always lies INSIDE the triangle, for every type of triangle.
questions.explanation: Median definition; medians meet at the centroid, which is always inside.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AD is a median and G is the centroid. If AG = 6 cm, find GD and the full length AD.
questions.answer: The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex, so AG : GD = 2 : 1. Since AG = 6 cm corresponds to 2 parts, one part = 3 cm, so GD = 3 cm. The full median AD = AG + GD = 6 + 3 = 9 cm.
questions.explanation: Use AG:GD = 2:1, so GD = AG/2 and AD = AG + GD.

questions.question: Define an altitude of a triangle and describe where the orthocentre lies for (a) an acute triangle, (b) a right triangle, (c) an obtuse triangle.
questions.answer: An ALTITUDE is the perpendicular segment drawn from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. The three altitudes meet at the ORTHOCENTRE (H). (a) In an acute triangle, H lies INSIDE the triangle. (b) In a right triangle, H lies AT the vertex of the right angle. (c) In an obtuse triangle, H lies OUTSIDE the triangle.
questions.explanation: Altitude definition plus the three positions of the orthocentre.

questions.question: What is the circumcentre of a triangle? State the property that makes it the centre of the circumcircle.
questions.answer: The CIRCUMCENTRE (O) is the point of concurrency of the three PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS of the sides of a triangle. Because every point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from the two ends of that side, O is equidistant from all three vertices: OA = OB = OC = R. A circle with centre O and radius R therefore passes through all three vertices - this is the circumcircle, and R is the circumradius.
questions.explanation: O is equidistant from the three vertices, so it is the centre of the circle through them.

questions.question: Explain why the incentre of a triangle is equidistant from all three sides, and state what circle has the incentre as its centre.
questions.answer: The incentre I is the point where the three internal ANGLE BISECTORS meet. Every point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the two arms of that angle. Since I lies on the bisector of angle B, it is equidistant from sides BA and BC; since it lies on the bisector of angle C, it is equidistant from CB and CA. Combining, I is equidistant from all three sides. That common perpendicular distance is the inradius r, and the circle with centre I and radius r that touches all three sides from inside is the INCIRCLE.
questions.explanation: Angle-bisector equidistance property gives equal distances to all three sides; the incircle is centred at I.

questions.question: In a right triangle the right angle is at C and the hypotenuse AB = 10 cm. State where the orthocentre and the circumcentre lie, and find the circumradius.
questions.answer: In a right triangle, the two legs are themselves altitudes and meet at the right-angle vertex, so the ORTHOCENTRE is at C. The CIRCUMCENTRE is the mid-point of the hypotenuse AB. The circumradius equals half the hypotenuse, so R = AB/2 = 10/2 = 5 cm.
questions.explanation: Right triangle: orthocentre at right-angle vertex; circumcentre at mid-point of hypotenuse; R = half the hypotenuse.

questions.question: Make a table comparing the four classic centres of a triangle: name of centre, the three lines that meet there, its symbol, one key property, and whether it always lies inside the triangle.
questions.answer:
Centroid (G): the three MEDIANS meet; key property - divides each median 2:1 from the vertex; ALWAYS inside.
Orthocentre (H): the three ALTITUDES meet; key property - foot of the perpendicular heights; NOT always inside (acute: inside, right: at right-angle vertex, obtuse: outside).
Circumcentre (O): the three PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS meet; key property - equidistant from the three vertices (OA=OB=OC=R), centre of the circumcircle; NOT always inside (acute: inside, right: mid-point of hypotenuse, obtuse: outside).
Incentre (I): the three ANGLE BISECTORS meet; key property - equidistant from the three sides (inradius r), centre of the incircle; ALWAYS inside.
questions.explanation: Systematic comparison of the four centres, their generating lines, symbols, properties and positions.

questions.question: The vertices of a triangle are A(2, 3), B(4, 7) and C(6, 2). Find the coordinates of the centroid.
questions.explanation: Average the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates of the three vertices.

questions.question: Which triangle has all four of its classic centres at the same point, and why?
questions.answer: The EQUILATERAL triangle. In an equilateral triangle, by symmetry, the median, altitude, perpendicular bisector and angle bisector drawn from any vertex are all the SAME line. Since the four sets of special lines coincide, their points of concurrency also coincide - so the centroid, orthocentre, circumcentre and incentre are one and the same point.
questions.explanation: Equilateral symmetry makes the four sets of lines identical, so their centres coincide.

questions.question: State the method to test whether three given lines are concurrent.
questions.answer: Find the point of intersection of any two of the three lines. Then substitute that point into the equation of the third line (or check geometrically whether it lies on the third line). If the point lies on the third line, the three lines are concurrent and that point is the point of concurrency; otherwise they are not concurrent.
questions.explanation: Intersect two, test the third.

questions.question: Why can we not call just two lines 'concurrent'?
questions.answer: Concurrency describes three or more lines all passing through one common point. Two distinct lines that meet simply intersect at a single point - that is the ordinary case of intersecting lines and needs no special name. The interesting, special property arises only when a THIRD (or further) line also passes through that same point. Hence at least three lines are needed before we speak of concurrency.
questions.explanation: Concurrency needs at least three lines.

questions.question: Show that the lines x + y = 4, x - y = 0 and y = 2 are concurrent.
questions.answer: First intersect x - y = 0 (i.e. y = x) with y = 2: this gives x = 2, y = 2, so the point is (2, 2). Now test the third line x + y = 4: substituting (2, 2) gives 2 + 2 = 4, which is true. Since (2, 2) lies on all three lines, they are concurrent, with point of concurrency (2, 2).
questions.explanation: Point (2,2) satisfies all three equations.

questions.question: Name the four triples of lines in a triangle that are always concurrent.
questions.answer: In any triangle, the following four sets of three lines are always concurrent: (1) the three MEDIANS (meeting at the centroid), (2) the three ALTITUDES (meeting at the orthocentre), (3) the three PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS of the sides (meeting at the circumcentre), and (4) the three internal ANGLE BISECTORS (meeting at the incentre).
questions.explanation: Medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors.

questions.question: Define a median of a triangle and state how many medians a triangle has.
questions.answer: A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side. A triangle has exactly three medians, one drawn from each of its three vertices.
questions.explanation: Vertex to mid-point of opposite side; three medians.

questions.question: State two important facts about the centroid of a triangle.
questions.answer: (1) The centroid is the point where the three medians of the triangle meet, and it always lies inside the triangle. (2) The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex, and it is the centre of gravity (centre of mass) of a uniform triangular lamina.
questions.explanation: Meeting point of medians; 2:1 property / centre of gravity.

questions.question: Explain why a single median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
questions.answer: A median from a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side splits that side into two equal halves. The two smaller triangles formed share the same vertex (and hence the same height from that vertex to the opposite side) and have equal bases (the two halves of the side). Since area = 1/2 * base * height and both base and height are equal for the two parts, the two triangles have equal area.
questions.explanation: Equal bases and shared height give equal areas.

questions.question: On median AD of a triangle, the centroid G satisfies AG = 8 cm. Find GD and AD.
questions.answer: The centroid divides the median in the ratio AG:GD = 2:1. So GD is half of AG: GD = 8/2 = 4 cm. The full median AD = AG + GD = 8 + 4 = 12 cm.
questions.explanation: GD = AG/2 = 4 cm; AD = 12 cm.

questions.question: A median BE of a triangle measures 21 cm. Find the distances BG and GE, where G is the centroid.
questions.answer: The centroid is two-thirds of the way along the median from the vertex, so BG = (2/3)*21 = 14 cm, and GE = (1/3)*21 = 7 cm. (Check: BG:GE = 14:7 = 2:1, and BG + GE = 21 cm.)

questions.question: Find the centroid of the triangle whose vertices are A(-2, 3), B(4, -1) and C(1, 7).
questions.explanation: Average the coordinates: G = (1, 3).

questions.question: Two vertices of a triangle are A(1, 2) and B(5, 4), and its centroid is G(3, 3). Find the third vertex C.
questions.answer: Let C = (x, y). The centroid formula gives (1 + 5 + x)/3 = 3 and (2 + 4 + y)/3 = 3. From the first: 6 + x = 9, so x = 3. From the second: 6 + y = 9, so y = 3. Therefore C = (3, 3).
questions.explanation: Solve the centroid equations for the unknown vertex: C = (3, 3).

questions.question: Define an altitude of a triangle and name the point where the three altitudes meet.
questions.answer: An altitude of a triangle is the perpendicular segment drawn from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent; their common point is called the ORTHOCENTRE (denoted H).
questions.explanation: Perpendicular from vertex to opposite side; meet at the orthocentre.

questions.question: Describe the position of the orthocentre for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
questions.answer: For an ACUTE triangle (all angles less than 90 degrees), the orthocentre lies inside the triangle. For a RIGHT triangle, the orthocentre lies exactly at the vertex of the right angle, because the two legs are themselves altitudes and meet there. For an OBTUSE triangle (one angle greater than 90 degrees), the orthocentre lies outside the triangle, and the sides have to be extended for the altitudes to meet.
questions.explanation: Acute: inside; right: right-angle vertex; obtuse: outside.

questions.question: How does an altitude differ from a median of a triangle?
questions.answer: An altitude is drawn from a vertex PERPENDICULAR to the opposite side; it need not reach the mid-point of that side. A median is drawn from a vertex to the MID-POINT of the opposite side; it need not be perpendicular to that side. So an altitude is defined by perpendicularity and a median by bisecting the opposite side. They coincide only in special cases (for example, from the apex of an isosceles triangle, or in an equilateral triangle).
questions.explanation: Altitude = perpendicular; median = to mid-point; differ in general.

questions.question: Define the perpendicular bisector of a side and name the point where the three perpendicular bisectors meet.
questions.answer: The perpendicular bisector of a side is the line that passes through the mid-point of that side and is perpendicular to it. The three perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent; their common point is the CIRCUMCENTRE (denoted O).
questions.explanation: Through mid-point and perpendicular; meet at the circumcentre.

questions.question: Prove (in words) that the circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices.
questions.answer: The circumcentre O lies on the perpendicular bisector of each side. A key property of the perpendicular bisector of a segment is that every point on it is equidistant from the two ends of that segment. Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, it is equidistant from B and C (OB = OC). Since O lies on the perpendicular bisector of CA, it is equidistant from C and A (OC = OA). Combining, OA = OB = OC. So O is equidistant from all three vertices; this common distance is the circumradius R.
questions.explanation: O lies on all three perpendicular bisectors, so OA = OB = OC.

questions.question: What is the circumcircle of a triangle, and where is its centre for a right triangle?
questions.answer: The circumcircle is the unique circle that passes through all three vertices of the triangle; its centre is the circumcentre O and its radius is the circumradius R (with OA = OB = OC = R). For a right triangle, the circumcentre is at the mid-point of the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle and R equals half the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: Circle through all vertices; centre at mid-point of hypotenuse for a right triangle.

questions.question: A right triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. Find its circumradius.
questions.answer: First find the hypotenuse using Pythagoras: hypotenuse = sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15 cm. In a right triangle the circumcentre is the mid-point of the hypotenuse, so the circumradius R = 15/2 = 7.5 cm.
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse = 15 cm; R = half of it = 7.5 cm.

questions.question: Define an internal angle bisector and name the point where the three of them meet.
questions.answer: An internal angle bisector of a triangle is the line segment (or ray) drawn from a vertex into the interior that divides the angle at that vertex into two equal parts. The three internal angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent; their common point is the INCENTRE (denoted I).
questions.explanation: Divides an angle in half; the three meet at the incentre.

questions.question: Explain why the incentre is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle.
questions.answer: The incentre I lies on all three internal angle bisectors. A key property of an angle bisector is that every point on it is equidistant from the two arms (sides) of the angle. Since I lies on the bisector of angle A, it is equidistant from sides AB and AC. Since I lies on the bisector of angle B, it is equidistant from sides BA and BC. Combining these, I is equidistant from all three sides AB, BC and CA. This common perpendicular distance is the inradius r.
questions.explanation: I lies on all three angle bisectors, so it is equidistant from all sides.

questions.question: What is the incircle of a triangle, and why does the incentre always lie inside the triangle?
questions.answer: The incircle is the circle that touches (is tangent to) all three sides of the triangle from inside; its centre is the incentre I and its radius is the inradius r. The incentre always lies inside the triangle because the internal angle bisectors all head into the interior, so their common point is interior; also, a circle that must touch all three sides from within can only have its centre inside the triangle.
questions.explanation: Incircle touches all three sides; incentre must be interior.

questions.question: State the equidistance property used to locate (a) the circumcentre and (b) the incentre.
questions.answer: (a) Circumcentre: it uses the property that every point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from the two end-points (vertices) of that side - so the circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices. (b) Incentre: it uses the property that every point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the two arms of the angle - so the incentre is equidistant from all three sides.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular bisector -> equidistant from vertices; angle bisector -> equidistant from sides.

questions.question: Explain why all four classic centres coincide in an equilateral triangle.
questions.answer: In an equilateral triangle all three sides are equal and all angles are 60 degrees. Because of this symmetry, the line drawn from any vertex serves simultaneously as the median (it reaches the mid-point of the opposite side), the altitude (it is perpendicular to that side), the perpendicular bisector of that side, and the bisector of the vertex angle. Thus the four sets of special lines are actually the SAME three lines. Since the lines coincide, their points of concurrency - the centroid, orthocentre, circumcentre and incentre - all coincide at a single point.
questions.explanation: The four sets of lines are identical, so their centres coincide.

questions.question: What is the Euler line, and which centres lie on it?
questions.answer: The Euler line of a triangle is the straight line that passes through three of its centres: the centroid G, the orthocentre H and the circumcentre O. These three points are always collinear (they lie on one line), and the centroid divides the segment from the circumcentre to the orthocentre in the ratio OG:GH = 1:2. The incentre does not generally lie on the Euler line (except when the triangle is equilateral, where all centres coincide).
questions.explanation: Line through G, H, O; OG:GH = 1:2; incentre generally off it.

questions.question: For an obtuse triangle, state the position (inside/outside/on the triangle) of each of the four centres.
questions.answer: In an obtuse triangle: the CENTROID lies inside; the INCENTRE lies inside; the ORTHOCENTRE lies outside the triangle; and the CIRCUMCENTRE lies outside the triangle. So two centres (centroid and incentre) stay inside while the orthocentre and circumcentre move outside.
questions.explanation: Centroid and incentre inside; orthocentre and circumcentre outside.

questions.question: In a right triangle ABC with the right angle at B and AC = 26 cm, find the circumradius and state where the orthocentre lies.
questions.answer: Since angle B = 90 degrees, AC is the hypotenuse. The circumcentre is at the mid-point of the hypotenuse AC, so the circumradius R = AC/2 = 26/2 = 13 cm. The orthocentre lies at the right-angle vertex B.
questions.explanation: R = half the hypotenuse = 13 cm; orthocentre at B.

questions.question: Describe how to construct the centroid of a given triangle using a ruler and compasses.
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the mid-point of one side (say BC) - for example by drawing its perpendicular bisector or by measurement - and join it to the opposite vertex A to draw the median AD. Step 2: Similarly find the mid-point of another side and draw the second median from its opposite vertex. Step 3: The point where these two medians intersect is the centroid G. (Drawing the third median is a useful check - it will pass through the same point.)
questions.explanation: Draw two medians; their intersection is the centroid.

questions.question: A median of a triangle has length 24 cm. A student marks the centroid on it. Find (a) the distance from the vertex to the centroid and (b) the distance from the centroid to the mid-point of the opposite side.
questions.answer: The centroid divides the median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex, i.e. it is two-thirds of the way from the vertex. (a) Distance from the vertex to the centroid = (2/3)*24 = 16 cm. (b) Distance from the centroid to the mid-point of the opposite side = (1/3)*24 = 8 cm. (Check: 16 + 8 = 24 cm and 16:8 = 2:1.)
questions.explanation: Vertex-to-centroid = 2/3 of 24 = 16 cm; centroid-to-side = 1/3 of 24 = 8 cm.

questions.question: A student says: 'The orthocentre and the centroid are always the same point.' Is this correct? Justify.
questions.answer: No, this is not correct in general. The centroid (meeting of the medians) and the orthocentre (meeting of the altitudes) are different points for most triangles, because medians and altitudes are different lines. They coincide only in special triangles such as the equilateral triangle, where by symmetry all four centres fall on one point. For a general scalene triangle the centroid and orthocentre are distinct (though both, with the circumcentre, lie on the Euler line).
questions.explanation: Only equal for equilateral triangles; distinct in general.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, D, E and F are the mid-points of BC, CA and AB respectively. Name the three medians and state their point of concurrency.
questions.answer: The three medians are AD (from vertex A to the mid-point D of BC), BE (from vertex B to the mid-point E of CA) and CF (from vertex C to the mid-point F of AB). These three medians are concurrent; their common point is the centroid G of the triangle.
questions.explanation: Medians AD, BE, CF meet at the centroid.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Three straight lines are given: L1: x + y = 6, L2: x - y = 2, and L3: 2x - y = 5.

(i) Find the point where L1 and L2 intersect.
(ii) Does that point lie on L3?
(iii) Are the three lines concurrent?
(iv) State the definition of concurrent lines.
questions.answer:
(i) Solving L1 and L2: adding x + y = 6 and x - y = 2 gives 2x = 8, so x = 4; then y = 6 - 4 = 2. Intersection point = (4, 2).
(ii) Substitute (4, 2) into L3: 2(4) - 2 = 8 - 2 = 6, but L3 requires 5. Since 6 is not equal to 5, the point (4, 2) does NOT lie on L3.
(iii) No - because the intersection of L1 and L2 does not lie on L3, the three lines are not concurrent.
(iv) Three or more lines are concurrent if they all pass through one common point (the point of concurrency).
questions.explanation: Test concurrency by intersecting two lines and checking the third.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In triangle ABC, the medians AD, BE and CF meet at the centroid G. It is given that AD = 18 cm and BG = 10 cm.

(i) State the ratio in which G divides each median.
(ii) Find AG and GD.
(iii) Find GE.
(iv) Where does the centroid always lie?
questions.answer:
(i) The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1, measured from the vertex.
(ii) On AD: AG = (2/3)*18 = 12 cm and GD = (1/3)*18 = 6 cm.
(iii) On BE: BG = 10 cm is the 2-part, so GE = BG/2 = 5 cm.
(iv) The centroid always lies inside the triangle.
questions.explanation: Apply the 2:1 property to each median.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A triangle has vertices P(2, 1), Q(6, 3) and R(4, 8).

(i) Write the formula for the centroid.
(ii) Find the centroid of triangle PQR.
(iii) If the centroid were the origin instead, what would P + Q + R (sum of coordinates) have to be?
(iv) Does the centroid lie inside triangle PQR?
questions.answer:
(i) Centroid G = ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3).
(ii) G = ((2+6+4)/3, (1+3+8)/3) = (12/3, 12/3) = (4, 4).
(iii) For the centroid to be the origin (0,0), the sums must be x1+x2+x3 = 0 and y1+y2+y3 = 0; that is, the coordinate sums would each have to be 0.
(iv) Yes - the centroid always lies inside the triangle, so it lies inside triangle PQR.
questions.explanation: Use the centroid coordinate formula.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent at the orthocentre H.

(i) Define an altitude.
(ii) Where is the orthocentre of an acute triangle?
(iii) Where is the orthocentre of a right triangle?
(iv) Where is the orthocentre of an obtuse triangle?
questions.answer:
(i) An altitude is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side.
(ii) In an acute triangle, the orthocentre lies inside the triangle.
(iii) In a right triangle, the orthocentre lies at the vertex of the right angle.
(iv) In an obtuse triangle, the orthocentre lies outside the triangle.
questions.explanation: Orthocentre position depends on the triangle type.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of triangle ABC meet at the circumcentre O. A circle centred at O passes through A, B and C.

(i) What is the name of this circle?
(ii) Why is OA = OB = OC?
(iii) What is this common distance called?
(iv) Where does O lie if the triangle is right-angled?
questions.answer:
(i) It is called the circumcircle (circumscribed circle) of the triangle.
(ii) O lies on the perpendicular bisector of each side. Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from the two vertices at its ends, so OA = OB (from side AB's bisector), OB = OC, and OA = OC; hence OA = OB = OC.
(iii) This common distance is the circumradius R.
(iv) If the triangle is right-angled, O lies at the mid-point of the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: Circumcentre is equidistant from vertices; centre of the circumcircle.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The internal angle bisectors of triangle ABC meet at the incentre I. A circle centred at I touches all three sides.

(i) What is the name of this circle?
(ii) Why is I equidistant from all three sides?
(iii) What is the common distance called?
(iv) Where does the incentre lie for any triangle?
questions.answer:
(i) It is called the incircle (inscribed circle) of the triangle.
(ii) I lies on all three angle bisectors. Every point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the two arms of that angle, so I is equidistant from each pair of sides meeting at the bisected vertices; combining, I is equidistant from all three sides.
(iii) The common perpendicular distance is the inradius r.
(iv) The incentre always lies inside the triangle, for every type of triangle.
questions.explanation: Incentre is equidistant from sides; centre of the incircle; always inside.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Four students each locate a different centre of the same triangle: the centroid, orthocentre, circumcentre and incentre.

(i) Which centre is the centre of gravity?
(ii) Which centre is the centre of the circumcircle?
(iii) Which centre is the centre of the incircle?
(iv) In which triangle would all four students mark the SAME point?
questions.answer:
(i) The centroid is the centre of gravity of the triangular lamina.
(ii) The circumcentre is the centre of the circumcircle.
(iii) The incentre is the centre of the incircle.
(iv) In an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide, so all four students would mark the same point.
questions.explanation: Match each centre to its role; equilateral triangle makes them coincide.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In any triangle, three of the centres are always collinear.

(i) Name the three collinear centres.
(ii) What is this line called?
(iii) In what ratio does the centroid divide the segment joining the circumcentre and orthocentre?
(iv) Which centre generally does NOT lie on this line?
questions.answer:
(i) The centroid (G), the orthocentre (H) and the circumcentre (O) are always collinear.
(ii) The line through them is called the Euler line.
(iii) The centroid divides the segment from the circumcentre to the orthocentre in the ratio OG:GH = 1:2.
(iv) The incentre generally does not lie on the Euler line (except in the equilateral case, where all centres coincide).
questions.explanation: Euler line contains G, H, O with OG:GH = 1:2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A right-angled triangle ABC has the right angle at C, with legs CA = 8 cm and CB = 6 cm.

(i) Find the length of the hypotenuse AB.
(ii) Where is the circumcentre located?
(iii) Find the circumradius.
(iv) Where is the orthocentre located?
questions.answer:
(i) By Pythagoras, AB = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = sqrt(64 + 36) = sqrt(100) = 10 cm.
(ii) The circumcentre is at the mid-point of the hypotenuse AB.
(iii) The circumradius R = AB/2 = 10/2 = 5 cm.
(iv) The orthocentre is at the right-angle vertex C.
questions.explanation: Right triangle: circumcentre at mid-hypotenuse, R = half hypotenuse, orthocentre at right angle.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student is asked which lines to construct to find each centre of a triangle.

(i) Which lines locate the centroid?
(ii) Which lines locate the circumcentre?
(iii) Which lines locate the incentre?
(iv) Which lines locate the orthocentre?
questions.answer:
(i) The medians (join each vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side); their intersection is the centroid.
(ii) The perpendicular bisectors of the sides; their intersection is the circumcentre.
(iii) The internal angle bisectors; their intersection is the incentre.
(iv) The altitudes (perpendiculars from each vertex to the opposite side); their intersection is the orthocentre.
questions.explanation: Each centre comes from its own set of concurrent lines.
